title: Solution Design & Architecture
headline: Start with the job. Then choose the system.
deck: A powerful model is only one component. Design around the business outcome, the binding constraint, and the feedback that tells you whether the system worked.
diagramNote: Select a stage to see what belongs there. Feedback changes the next version of the system.
nodes: Ingest
Normalize ticket text and CRM metadata. Validate required fields before reasoning begins.
Process
Classify intent, select a resolution path, and use tools only where the job requires them.
Deliver
Validate the response or action. Enforce refund limits in code before executing a payment.
Measure outcome
Track closed, reopened, and escalated tickets. A fluent reply is not proof that the issue was resolved.
Improve
Use quality, cost, latency, user feedback, and drift signals to revise prompts, routing, or the workflow.
learnings: Translate the business request into four concrete parts.

Write down the input, the processing needed, the output, and the feedback signal. “Automate support” is too broad. “Turn ticket text and customer context into a validated resolution, then track reopenings” exposes the actual engineering work.
The binding constraint should decide the architecture.

A latency target, an audit requirement, or a strict cost ceiling can rule out an attractive design. Identify which requirement is mandatory before comparing models or adding agents. A complex task can still have a predictable sequence.
Can an LLM do it is a different question from should it do it.

Keep exact lookups, fixed rules, and enforceable limits in ordinary code. Use the model where language interpretation or judgment adds value. In the support example, a maximum refund is a runtime condition, not a request for the model to behave responsibly.
Business value has several dimensions that can conflict.

Efficiency reduces effort per unit; transformation creates a capability; productivity expands human output; cost concerns total spend; performance concerns service targets. A research-heavy agent may create new capability while worsening turnaround time. State the priority explicitly.
Close the loop using outcomes, not just model output.

Measure whether work was accepted, corrected, reopened, or escalated. Combine that with quality checks and operational measurements. The same failure may require a better prompt, different retrieval, a simpler workflow, or a human handoff; feedback tells you which path to investigate.
tableTitle: Match the business goal to the evidence
tableRows: A feature with no useful outcome
Savings that shift work to humans
caseTitle: Insurance summaries under a tight deadline
caseProblem: The lesson proposes 50,000 standardized summaries per day, a response target under three seconds, and a quality threshold above 95%. Treat those figures as scenario constraints, not measured results.
caseBefore: An open-ended multi-agent investigation adds coordination, variable paths, and extra reasoning to a predictable job.
caseAfter: Use a fixed extraction and template workflow, a bounded narrative step, and deterministic validation. Measure the actual latency and quality before claiming the SLA is met.
caseWhy: The task is known in advance. The design should spend its budget on the required output rather than on discovering the process.
flowTitle: Turn a request into an architecture decision
checklist: Write one sentence describing a successful business outcome.
Record the mandatory latency, quality, cost, and audit limits.
Name the feedback signal that would reveal hidden rework.
caveat: The examples are the instructor’s scenarios. SLA figures are design targets; they do not establish measured production performance.

title: Architecture Patterns
headline: Use autonomy only where the path is unknown.
deck: Distinguish a bounded augmented LLM, a predefined workflow, and a runtime agent loop. Then decide whether specialists earn the cost of coordination.
diagramNote: Select a role. In this topology, the coordinator owns delegation, aggregation, and recovery.
nodes: Business request
The request includes the objective, quality criteria, and operating limits.
Coordinator
Decompose only when necessary, pass sufficient context, aggregate results, and handle failures.
Specialist A
A narrow role with only the context and tools needed for its assigned work.
Specialist B
An independent specialist can run concurrently when its inputs do not depend on another result.
Specialist C
In the lesson’s hub-and-spoke design, specialist communication returns through the coordinator.
learnings: Known steps belong in a workflow.

Prompt chaining runs a defined sequence. Routing selects a predefined branch. Parallelization handles independent work. These patterns remain workflows even when each stage uses a capable model. Complexity alone does not require runtime autonomy.
Use an agent when findings determine the next action.

An investigation may need to inspect logs, form a hypothesis, call another tool, and revise its plan. That perceive–think–act–observe loop buys flexibility, but also introduces variable latency, token use, and execution paths.
An augmented LLM can be enough for a bounded job.

Adding retrieved knowledge or a limited tool capability can solve a focused request without building a general planner. Treat this as a design pattern, not a promise that tool use always fits into one API round trip. Hybrids are possible when only one stage needs autonomy.
Multiple agents need a reason stronger than specialization sounds useful.

A coordinator adds hops, context duplication, and failure handling. Specialists make sense when their distinct responsibilities or independent work justify that overhead. If code can express the decomposition reliably, a fixed workflow may be simpler.
Tool scope is part of architecture quality.

A role with many irrelevant tools pays in context size and selection ambiguity. Give each role the capabilities its work requires. Remove unused capabilities before adding more instructions to compensate for a bloated choice set.
caseTitle: Five known stages do not need a planner
caseProblem: The claims-processing scenario already specifies extraction, validation, classification, routing, and summarization. It also requires predictable turnaround, an audit trail, and controlled cost.
caseBefore: A general agent repeatedly decides which of the same five steps to perform next.
caseAfter: Express the five stages in a fixed workflow, with explicit branch conditions and checks. Benchmark the proposed sub-five-second target instead of assuming it follows from the pattern.
caseWhy: The uncertainty is in interpreting claim content, not in discovering the overall sequence.
flow: Need multiple known steps? Use a workflow
Need runtime discovery? Add an agent loop
Keep the smallest design that passes
checklist: Separate uncertainty in the data from uncertainty in the process.
Draw dependencies before parallelizing any stages.
Measure the cost and latency of each coordinator hop.
caveat: The pattern boundaries are teaching abstractions. Real systems can combine them, and the hub-and-spoke restriction describes this topology rather than every possible agent design.

title: Decomposition & Business Value
headline: Split the work where a boundary earns its keep.
deck: Functional, data, and temporal decomposition are useful lenses. Extra boundaries become harmful when they repeat context, add handoffs, or obscure the business objective.
diagramTitle: Three lenses on the same job
diagramNote: Select a lens. These are alternative ways to reason about boundaries; they can be combined deliberately.
nodes: One business job
Start with a single outcome and its mandatory operating constraints.
By function
Split by capability: extract, classify, validate, or summarize.
By data
Split by modality or source when inputs need different processing.
By time
Split by phase: intake, assessment, human review, and final decision.
Check boundaries
For every handoff, compare the benefit against repeated context, coordination, and added failure modes.
learnings: Choose decomposition based on the shape of the work.

Functional boundaries separate different capabilities. Data boundaries separate inputs that need different treatment. Temporal boundaries separate stages with different responsibilities. Naming the lens makes a design easier to explain than inventing one agent per noun.
A boundary is a cost as well as a convenience.

Every new role can add serialization, context transfer, orchestration, and recovery. If several stages repeatedly read the same document and do closely related reasoning, consolidating them may improve latency without removing the actual work.
Parallelize independence, not a diagram that looks parallel.

A stage that needs another stage’s output cannot safely run at the same time merely to satisfy a deadline. Likewise, caching does not remove first-pass coordination overhead. Diagnose the source of delay before choosing a familiar optimization.
Make competing business goals explicit.

Efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and service performance pull in different directions. A cheaper model may require more review; a richer investigation may take longer. Explain which goal is binding and what evidence would justify the tradeoff.
Probabilistic systems need population-level operating checks.

Measure quality over representative requests and meaningful slices, monitor changes, and provide graceful degradation or escalation. A routing confidence signal needs calibration against outcomes; a model’s unsupported self-rating is not a reliable guarantee.
tableRows: Does it need a distinct capability or check?
Do these inputs require different handling?
Does responsibility change at this phase?
Are handoffs repeating the same context?
caseTitle: A legal review misses its latency target
caseProblem: The lesson’s five-agent review takes 45 seconds against a 20-second target. Extraction, risk analysis, and compliance checks repeatedly use the same contract.
caseBefore: Keep all five boundaries, add caching, or upgrade every model without locating the delay.
caseAfter: Consolidate closely related work that shares context. Keep genuinely independent stages parallel and preserve required validation. Measure the new critical path.
caseWhy: Reducing needless handoffs addresses the architectural cause. It does not guarantee the target without a benchmark.
checklist: Label each stage as functional, data-based, or temporal.
Mark repeated context and dependencies on the diagram.
Record the quality floor before reducing steps for speed.
caveat: The timing figures are illustrative. Confidence-based routing is useful only when its signal has been validated; raw model self-confidence is insufficient.

title: Model Selection & System Prompts
headline: Match capability to the task. Make behavior explicit.
deck: Model choice and prompt design solve different problems. Route by demonstrated capability, describe judgment precisely, and enforce hard limits outside the model.
diagramNote: Select a route. Model families here describe the lesson’s relative tiers, not a current pricing or compatibility guide.
nodes: Incoming task
Classify the task using explicit criteria and a routing approach validated on representative cases.
Fast / narrow
Use a lower-cost tier for bounded work only when evaluations show it meets the required quality.
General work
Use a workhorse tier for routine reasoning and tool-assisted resolution.
Hard / ambiguous
Reserve stronger capability or additional reasoning for tasks that justify the cost and latency.
Validate / escalate
Check outputs and actions, and escalate failures rather than treating routing as a guarantee.
learnings: The strongest model is not automatically the best system choice.

Compare task complexity, the latency budget, and the cost ceiling. The lesson uses Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus as relative tiers, but the deciding evidence should be performance on your task. A familiar family name is not a substitute for evaluation.
Tiering works when the difficult slice is identifiable.

A narrow classifier can route standard work to a general model and difficult cases to stronger capability. Keep a fallback path and measure errors within every route. Moving traffic to a cheaper tier is a quality-sensitive change, not merely a billing change.
Thinking effort is a tradeoff, not an always-on virtue.

Additional reasoning may help difficult tasks while consuming latency and output budget. Use it where a measured quality gain justifies the extra work. Exact model versions, effort settings, and API support need current documentation before implementation.
Replace vague adjectives with observable reporting criteria.

“Be thorough” can produce many low-value findings. A review prompt should name the issues worth reporting, what to skip, and the required evidence. Explicit severity and output rules reduce false positives that otherwise erode trust in the tool.
Separate behavioral guidance from hard enforcement.

A system prompt can define role, tool rules, response format, escalation, and prohibitions. Code should enforce mandatory limits and preconditions. Structured output can constrain shape; it does not establish that a claim or action is correct.
tableTitle: A useful system prompt has a contract
tableRows: Name the issue and cite evidence
Omit style issues handled by lint
Stop when a prerequisite is missing
caseProblem: A code review prompt asks for thorough, conservative analysis. The output fills with style suggestions and weak claims, so developers stop trusting it.
caseBefore: Increase model capability while leaving the reporting criteria vague.
caseAfter: Specify which defects matter, require concrete evidence, exclude lint-only style issues, and standardize the finding format. Compare false positives and missed issues on a fixed review set.
caseWhy: The behavior contract can be the bottleneck even when the model has sufficient capability.
checklist: Write report and skip criteria that a reviewer can apply.
Evaluate each proposed model route separately.
Move mandatory limits and prerequisites into runtime checks.
caveat: The video includes changing model and API details. This page retains the design principles and intentionally avoids presenting those version-specific claims as current specifications.

title: Prompt Engineering, Context & Caching
headline: Treat context as a budget, not a warehouse.
deck: Use examples to calibrate judgment, place evidence deliberately, and keep reusable prompt material stable. Cache reuse applies to a prefix, not to the whole answer.
diagramNote: Select a layer. The boundary separates reusable material from request-specific context.
nodes: Tool definitions
Keep applicable definitions stable and consistently ordered when the caching design depends on their prefix.
System instructions
Place stable behavior and policy guidance early. Avoid dynamic greetings or timestamps in this reusable region.
Reusable examples
Use a few diverse examples to calibrate formats and boundary judgments rather than filling the window.
Retrieved evidence
Include relevant, fresh evidence for this request. It is not automatically reusable across users and questions.
Current question
Put the specific task where it is easy to locate, with essential constraints reinforced when needed.
learnings: Add examples when they clarify a real ambiguity.

A simple task may need only an explicit instruction. A few carefully selected examples help with formatting and difficult boundary judgments. Prefer varied cases, including edge cases, over a large collection of near-duplicates. Examples guide behavior; they do not guarantee it.
A large context window does not make every token useful.

Irrelevant fields, verbose tool results, and repeated history compete with the evidence that matters. Budget instructions, examples, retrieved material, and output deliberately. Trim or summarize intermediate content while checking that essential facts survive.
Placement can affect whether important evidence is used.

The lesson describes lost-in-the-middle failures and recommends deliberate ordering: stable instructions early, relevant context close to the task, and a clear final question. Test placement on your workload rather than treating one ordering as universal.
Prompt caching reuses a stable prefix, not a previous answer.

Separate reusable tools, instructions, and examples from dynamic documents and queries. A cache read can be cheaper than processing the same input again, while writes and expiry affect the economics. Fresh input and generated output still have their own costs.
Progressive disclosure reduces irrelevant context.

Always-applicable guidance and on-demand skill bodies serve different purposes. Keep the small discovery description available and load detailed instructions when relevant. Deferring content reduces prompt load; it does not remove a capability or its authorization requirements.
tableRows: Reuse collapses after a prompt edit
A dynamic field entered the prefix
Only part of input is reusable
caseTitle: A cached prefix is only part of the bill
caseProblem: The lesson illustrates a request with 2,800 stable tokens and 3,000 fresh tokens. Only the stable portion is a candidate for cross-request reuse.
caseBefore: Assume a large discount on cached reads means the entire request becomes equally cheaper.
caseAfter: Account separately for the stable prefix’s writes and reads, the fresh input, and the generated output. Check traffic frequency and expiry before forecasting savings.
caseWhy: A large percentage saving on one bucket can be a modest saving on the complete workload.
flowTitle: Build and maintain a reusable prefix
flow: Keep dynamic fields after the boundary
checklist: Remove fields that cannot change the answer.
Put request timestamps and variable greetings outside the stable prefix.
Measure cache reads, writes, fresh input, and output separately.
caveat: Cache rates, minimum lengths, lifetime options, and model support change. The page teaches the accounting and placement principles, not current provider pricing.

title: RAG Pipelines, Chunking & Retrieval
headline: A better answer starts before the model sees it.
deck: Retrieval-augmented generation is a pipeline. Preserve document meaning, retrieve for the actual query, and diagnose the index when fresh content produces stale or generic answers.
diagramNote: Select a stage. The index links document preparation to query-time evidence selection.
nodes: Ingest
Parse the source while preserving headings, tables, document identity, and access metadata.
Chunk
Choose boundaries that preserve the meaning needed to answer a question.
Embed / index
Build searchable representations and metadata. Refresh them consistently when documents change.
Query
Interpret the current question, including exact identifiers and metadata constraints.
Retrieve
Use semantic, keyword, or hybrid matching, with filters appropriate to the document and user.
Rerank
Narrow a candidate pool to the evidence most relevant to the question, if the added step earns its cost.
Generate
Answer from the selected evidence and acknowledge when the required support is absent.
learnings: Chunking is a meaning-preservation decision.

Fixed-size chunks are simple but may cut an argument or clause. Semantic chunks follow topic changes. Structure-aware chunks respect headings, sections, tables, and legal clauses. Choose the boundary that preserves the relationships your questions depend on.
A fragment needs enough identity to stand alone.

A chunk saying revenue grew by three percent is ambiguous without the company and period. Contextual information can make a fragment interpretable before it is indexed. Preserve source identity and metadata so the answer can remain tied to the right document.
Semantic similarity and exact matching solve different problems.

Vector retrieval helps with related meanings. Keyword retrieval helps with contract numbers, names, and exact terms. Hybrid retrieval can combine them; metadata narrows the scope by date, document, tenant, or access context. Select based on query behavior.
More retrieved text is not automatically better evidence.

Reranking can reduce a broad candidate pool to a smaller, more useful set. That adds a step but can improve the signal passed to the generator and reduce context waste. Judge it against quality and latency, not simply the number of chunks returned.
After a corpus refresh, inspect retrieval before changing the model.

Look for stale embeddings, missing re-indexing, lost metadata, index synchronization failures, or parsing changes. If the correct evidence never reaches the model, a stronger model may only produce a more convincing unsupported answer.
tableRows: Answer does not fabricate a policy
caseTitle: A contract question gets a generic answer
caseProblem: In the lesson’s legal-document scenario, a question about one contract retrieves generic termination language rather than the relevant clause and its conditions.
caseBefore: Add a larger context window or ask the model to reason harder over the same weak evidence.
caseAfter: Preserve clause structure, add document identity, use exact-match signals alongside semantic retrieval, and filter to the intended contract. Inspect the retrieved evidence before judging generation.
caseWhy: The bottleneck is evidence selection. Generation can only be grounded in the material it receives.
checklist: Keep headings, document identity, and relevant metadata with chunks.
Test exact identifiers as well as semantic paraphrases.
Include questions whose answer is absent from the corpus.
caveat: The transcript’s local demonstration uses lexical TF-IDF retrieval. It should not be confused with a dense embedding model or a dedicated cross-encoder reranker.

title: MCP, Authentication & Capability Bloat
headline: A protocol connects tools. Authorization bounds them.
deck: Choose the integration mechanism, the identity, and the available capabilities separately. Then distinguish a large useful catalog from a role carrying powers it should never have.
diagramTitle: Three decisions at the integration boundary
diagramNote: Select a layer. Transport, identity, and tool visibility do not replace resource authorization.
nodes: Agent / client
The client has a defined role and a real user or service identity behind its actions.
Protocol
Use MCP when shared discovery and interoperability are useful; a direct API or CLI can fit a simpler integration.
Server
The server validates calls and provides the integration boundary; it must not blindly trust the model’s request.
Identity
Use appropriately scoped credentials and validate the token audience. Do not blindly forward incoming credentials downstream.
Capabilities
Expose only tools appropriate to the role, and keep secrets out of model context.
Resource checks
Authorize the actual user, action, and resource on every relevant call. Hiding a tool is not the whole permission model.
learnings: Use a protocol because the integration needs it.

MCP offers a common interface and capability discovery across clients. A direct API or CLI may be sufficient for one known integration. A specialist that exercises its own judgment is a different architectural choice from wrapping a tool endpoint.
Delegated identity should not silently become administrator access.

The lesson’s valet-key analogy highlights scoped access: a service must act within the caller’s authority. A broadly privileged shared credential can turn the server into a confused deputy that accesses another customer’s data.
Token handling belongs at a trust boundary.

Validate intended audience and scope; avoid blindly passing an incoming token to another service. Prefer credentials appropriate to the downstream action, keep secrets out of prompts, and enforce resource checks server-side. Tool descriptions cannot enforce those controls.
Capability bloat has four taxes.

Unnecessary tools increase selection ambiguity, token load, security exposure, and audit work. Audit usage, role fit, blast radius, privilege, and overlap. A capability outside the role should be removed, moved, or downscoped rather than merely surrounded with more warnings.
Deferred discovery solves context load, not excess authority.

A large catalog may be legitimate if all tools serve the role. On-demand discovery can reduce the material loaded upfront. An unused destructive tool is a different problem: deferring its description still leaves the capability reachable.
tableRows: Remove or move to the correct role
The role should not hold that power
caseTitle: A support role carries refund and deletion powers
caseProblem: The retail example gives a support agent 14 tools. Refund issuance and account deletion are unused and belong to separate finance and privacy workflows.
caseBefore: Keep both tools and add logging, confirmation prompts, or deferred loading.
caseAfter: Remove them from the support role and enforce the appropriate permissions on the server. Keep any required handoff to the responsible workflow explicit.
caseWhy: An audit trail records misuse after the fact. It does not justify granting an unrelated capability.
checklist: Map each tool to a concrete role responsibility.
Review credential scope and per-resource authorization separately.
Defer legitimate long-tail tools; remove unrelated powers.
caveat: Authentication and transport examples are lesson material, not a current MCP security specification. Verify the official protocol and identity documentation before implementing them.

title: Observability, Monitoring & Latency
headline: A green status code can hide a failed job.
deck: Trace the full request, monitor the service, and evaluate the outcome. Then spend latency where it buys necessary quality rather than optimizing the easiest number to improve.
diagramNote: Select a span. A correlation ID connects the request; each stage retains enough metadata to explain a failure.
nodes: Request trace
One root spans the user request and links retrieval, model calls, tools, and validation.
Retrieval
Record document IDs and index version so a bad answer can be traced back to selected evidence.
Model call
Record model, prompt/config version, token buckets, stop reason, request ID, and timing.
Tool call
Record tool name, outcome, error category, retries, and duration without leaking secrets.
Validation / outcome
Connect the trace to output checks, escalations, corrections, or other evidence of success.
learnings: Trace the unit of work rather than isolated API calls.

A user request may include retrieval, several model turns, tools, retries, and validation. Connect them under one trace. That makes it possible to distinguish a slow stage from a wrong-evidence stage instead of blaming the final model response.
Collect explanatory metadata without logging every sensitive payload.

Model and configuration versions, token buckets, timings, tool outcomes, and document IDs are useful baseline signals. Content logging needs deliberate sampling, access controls, and retention. Avoid putting user identifiers into high-cardinality metric labels.
Metrics detect; traces explain; quality evaluation judges usefulness.

Service latency, errors, and token counts can look healthy while answers deteriorate. Add representative quality checks and outcome signals such as escalations or corrections. A corpus refresh with rising escalations deserves retrieval and quality investigation even if HTTP status is green.
Separate time to first token from time to usable completion.

Streaming can make the interface feel responsive while total completion stays the same. A downstream system waiting for validated JSON still needs the complete result. Choose the latency measure that corresponds to the actual user or system requirement.
Optimize efficiency before deleting valuable reasoning or validation.

Try stable-prefix reuse, proven routing, and parallel independent lookups. Compare quality gains with cost and latency inside the real SLA. Removing verification from an overnight report may save seconds while damaging the objective that matters most.
tableRows: Where and why did it happen?
Slow tool, wrong document, repeated retry
Was the result useful and correct?
caseTitle: A latency optimization removes the valuable work
caseProblem: The lesson contrasts an interactive deadline with an overnight report. They have different latency budgets, so the same speed optimization can have different value.
caseBefore: Remove verification from the overnight report merely to reduce completion time.
caseAfter: Preserve quality checks when the deadline allows them. For an interactive path, measure the critical spans and optimize reuse, routing, or independent work while maintaining the quality floor.
caseWhy: Latency is a constraint to satisfy in context, not a number to minimize regardless of outcome.
flow: Keep only improvements inside the SLA
checklist: Connect retrieval, model, tool, and validation spans under one request.
Track quality alongside latency, errors, and token use.
Choose TTFT or completion latency according to the consumer.
caveat: The numeric quality and timing examples in the video are illustrations. Faster streaming does not by itself reduce the time to a validated final result.

title: AI Evaluation Metrics & Frameworks
headline: An average score can hide the failure that matters.
deck: Build a representative golden set, choose graders that fit the judgment, and gate changes on important slices. Evaluation should control releases, not decorate a report.
diagramTitle: From golden set to release gate
diagramNote: Select a stage. Graders feed slice-level evidence before a release decision is made.
nodes: Golden set
Version representative cases, difficult cases, missing evidence, and cases that must be refused or escalated.
Rules
Check exact values, schema, required nulls, and other criteria with deterministic answers.
Rubric judge
Use explicit criteria for nuanced judgments and calibrate the judge against human decisions.
Human review
Audit consequential cases, disagreements, and grader blind spots.
Slice analysis
Inspect document type, field criticality, and difficult classes instead of trusting only the aggregate.
Release gate
Compare against a fixed baseline and predeclared regression limits, accounting for noise.
learnings: Measure several dimensions without collapsing them into one score.

Accuracy, latency, cost, safety, and security answer different questions. A fast, cheap system may still fail a critical accuracy or safety requirement. Use traces for operational measures and targeted cases for judgments that logs alone cannot establish.
Stratification reveals what a headline hides.

A high overall score can coexist with poor performance on a rare but important document type. Slice by task, field, document class, and consequence. Oversample critical cases for inspection; keep the distinction between diagnostic coverage and traffic-weighted performance clear.
A golden set needs realistic variety, not just more rows.

Include representative production cases, edge cases, absent values, and cases requiring refusal or escalation. Version the set and handle sensitive examples deliberately. Adding thousands of similar easy cases does not repair a missing high-risk slice.
Match the grader to the kind of truth being checked.

Use rules for exact values and structure, a model with an explicit rubric for nuanced judgments, and humans for consequential audits and disagreements. A structured pass/fail response is useful only when the rubric and the grader are calibrated.
Measure the noise floor before declaring improvement.

Repeat the unchanged baseline to see how much results vary. Small samples and a few flipped judgments can create apparent wins. Predeclare overall and slice-level limits so a release cannot hide a severe minority regression behind an improved average.
tableRows: Needs human calibration and bias checks
A threshold needs a justified sample
caseTitle: A document extractor looks excellent overall
caseProblem: The lesson describes extraction across many document types. The aggregate score conceals a weak minority type whose fields are operationally important.
caseBefore: Accept the headline metric or expand the dataset with more examples of the common easy types.
caseAfter: Stratify by document and field criticality, add the missing hard cases, use rules plus a calibrated judge, and block unacceptable slice regressions.
caseWhy: Coverage is a dataset design problem. A larger unrepresentative sample can make the misleading aggregate look more convincing.
checklist: Add missing-value and absent-evidence cases to the golden set.
Publish critical slice scores next to the aggregate.
Audit grader disagreements before trusting a model judge.
caveat: A small demonstration with perfect grader agreement does not prove production accuracy. Audit percentages and regression thresholds in the lesson are scenario choices, not universal standards.

title: LLM A/B Testing & Failure Diagnosis
headline: Change one thing. Learn what actually caused the result.
deck: Use a fixed baseline and a controlled experiment, then diagnose failures across integration, prompts, grounding, and model capability. Roll out only after the evidence survives contact with traffic.
diagramNote: Select a stage. A failed gate returns to the baseline rather than becoming a new unexamined assumption.
nodes: Frozen baseline
Pin the prompt, examples, retrieval, model configuration, and validation used for comparison.
One variable
Change one component, such as chunking, so the observed difference has an interpretable cause.
Offline comparison
Use the same cases, graders, and predeclared measures. Repeat enough to understand variation.
Online exposure
Confirm on comparable traffic and a common time window using a gradual rollout.
Gate / rollback
Watch quality, critical slices, cost, latency, and errors. Keep a working rollback path.
learnings: An experiment needs a comparison contract.

Hold inputs or traffic assignment, time window, grading criteria, and success thresholds consistent. Change one variable at a time. If the model, prompt, and retrieval all change together, a new score does not tell you which component helped or hurt.
Start offline; confirm where the system will operate.

An offline golden set is a cheaper way to reject poor changes. A successful candidate still needs production confirmation on comparable traffic. Predeclare the evaluation window and avoid stopping at the first favorable fluctuation. No meaningful difference is a valid result.
Separate failure families before choosing a remedy.

Integration failures include missing data, tool errors, and post-processing. Prompt failures involve unclear or conflicting behavior. Hallucination involves unsupported claims. Model mismatch remains plausible when clean, sufficient context still exceeds the model’s ability.
Test the cheapest discriminating hypothesis first.

Quantify the symptom, list competing causes, inspect version differences and traces, and reproduce the suspected component in isolation. A bad answer after re-indexing should prompt a retrieval check; correct evidence that is ignored points toward prompt or use-of-context problems.
Target the weak slice and preserve reversibility.

If only a difficult class fails, evaluate selective routing or a better decomposition rather than upgrading every request. After a fix passes the original metric, expand traffic gradually while monitoring regressions and retaining the baseline for rollback.
tableTitle: Let the evidence choose the first investigation
tableRows: Only hard cases fail with clean context
caseProblem: The lesson’s coding-assistant example changes model, prompt, and chunk size together. Acceptance falls from an illustrative 34% to 27%.
caseBefore: Blame the new model because it is the most visible change.
caseAfter: Restore the baseline and isolate each change. In the example, larger chunks cause the regression; structure-aware code chunking addresses the evidence problem.
caseWhy: One-variable comparisons distinguish correlation from a useful causal explanation. The figures are teaching examples, not measured claims about a product.
flow: Fix and rerun the same metric
checklist: Pin the complete baseline configuration before an experiment.
Write success criteria and stopping rules in advance.
Reproduce the suspected component in isolation before upgrading everything.
caveat: The symptom-to-cause table gives investigation priorities, not certain diagnoses. Repeated comparisons and calibrated grading are still required for nondeterministic outputs.

title: Cost Optimization & Monitoring
headline: Optimize cost per useful outcome, not tokens in isolation.
deck: Separate fresh input, output, cache writes, and cache reads. Then use cache stability, proven tiering, context reduction, and asynchronous batching where the workload allows it.
diagramTitle: Four buckets feed the request bill
diagramNote: Select a bucket. Count each token in its applicable billing category, then relate the cost to accepted work.
nodes: Fresh input
Uncached request material has its own input rate. Smaller relevant context can reduce this bucket.
Output
Generated tokens have a separate rate. Length limits need truncation checks and quality validation.
Cache write
Creating reusable cached material is distinct from reading it; writes can have different economics.
Cache read
Repeated stable prefixes can shift input into the read bucket when reuse conditions hold.
Request cost
Sum the applicable token count times rate for each bucket; do not double-count cached input as fresh input.
Useful outcome
Track accepted work, quality, and latency next to spend. Lower cost with more failed work can be a false saving.
learnings: Unit economics explain what a growing total bill cannot.

A bill can rise because request volume grows, request mix changes, or each request becomes more expensive. Separate token buckets and track cost by request type. Relate spend to useful outcomes so retries and rework do not disappear from the analysis.
Cache health depends on prefix stability and traffic.

Dynamic fields early in the prompt, ordering changes, configuration drift, and expiry can reduce reuse. Inspect cache reads and writes rather than assuming a cached system remains healthy. Cache-read share of input tokens is different from the fraction of requests with a hit.
Tier and trim only while preserving the quality floor.

Move proven easy slices to lower-cost capability and remove irrelevant fields or history. Reduce retrieval depth with evidence from evaluations, not a blanket cut. Output caps need checks for truncation; a shorter answer is not automatically complete.
Batch work that genuinely tolerates asynchronous completion.

Independent overnight jobs can fit a batch API; an interactive user or a dependent tool loop usually needs a different path. Keep a durable request-to-result mapping using unique identifiers. Batch submission does not automatically execute a multi-turn tool workflow.
Monitor cost and drift even when you deploy nothing.

Watch cost per type, token composition, cache reuse, tail latency, errors/refusals, volume, and quality. Query mix, documents, and provider behavior can change without an application release. Scheduled golden-set checks and controlled migrations help expose that drift.

caseProblem: The lesson’s cache-health scenario drops from roughly 70% reuse to zero. Evaluation quality is unchanged, so the failure is economic rather than evidence of weaker reasoning.
caseBefore: Use a larger model, retrieve more documents, or move every request to batch processing.
caseAfter: Compare the serialized prefix. Move the variable greeting out of the reusable region and confirm that cache-read usage returns while quality and latency remain acceptable.
caseWhy: The first investigation should match the changed signal. A dynamic prefix explains cache collapse more directly than model capability does.
